## Skills
A skill is a set of local instructions to follow that is stored in a `SKILL.md` file. Below is the list of skills that can be used. Each entry includes a name, description, and a short path that can be expanded into an absolute path using the skill roots table.
### Skill roots
- `r0` = `/user/user1/harbor-runs/c14d98185e96/workspace/.codex/skills`
- `r1` = `/tmp/codex-home/skills/.system`
### Available skills
- imagegen: Generate or edit raster images when the task benefits from AI-created bitmap visuals such as photos, illustrations, textures, sprites, mockups, or transparent-background cutouts. Use when Codex should create a brand-new image, transform an existing image, or derive visual variants from references, and the output should be a bitmap asset rather than repo-native code or vector. Do not use when the task is better handled by editing existing SVG/vector/code-native assets, extending an established icon or logo system, or building the visual directly in HTML/CSS/canvas. (file: r1/imagegen/SKILL.md)
- openai-docs: Use for Codex models/pricing, scheduled tasks, skills, settings, setup, troubleshooting, customization, automations, and self-knowledge—including 'you,' 'your,' 'this app,' or 'this coding agent' when they refer to Codex—and for OpenAI APIs/products and ChatGPT Work. Also use for model choice/migration, prompting, SDKs, Responses, Realtime, agents, evals, and Chat/Work/Codex comparisons. Do not use for generic app/software tasks that merely mention Codex. (file: r1/openai-docs/SKILL.md)
- skill-creator: Create or update a Codex skill with appropriately scoped instructions and any needed supporting resources. (file: r1/skill-creator/SKILL.md)
- skill-installer: Install Codex skills into $CODEX_HOME/skills from a curated list or a GitHub repo path. Use when a user asks to list installable skills, install a curated skill, or install a skill from another repo (including private repos). (file: r1/skill-installer/SKILL.md)
- issue: Create or update a GitHub issue following verl project conventions. (file: r0/issue/SKILL.md)
- pr: Create or update a pull request following verl project conventions. (file: r0/pr/SKILL.md)
</skills_instructions><permissions instructions>

Your active mode changes only when new developer instructions with a different `<collaboration_mode>...</collaboration_mode>` change it; user requests or tool descriptions do not change mode by themselves. Known mode names are Default and Plan.

## request_user_input availability

Use the `request_user_input` tool only when it is listed in the available tools for this turn.

Use the `request_user_input` tool only for optional questions where the answer would materially improve the quality of the work.

If `request_user_input` returns no answers, continue with best judgment instead of asking again or treating the turn as blocked.

Never use the `request_user_input` tool for permission requests or permission-related escalations.
</collaboration_mode>

<multi_agent_role>You are `/root`, the primary agent in a team of agents collaborating to fulfill the user's goals.

At the start of your turn, you are the active agent.
You can spawn sub-agents to handle subtasks, and those sub-agents can spawn their own sub-agents.
All agents in the team, including the agents that you can assign tasks to, are equally intelligent and capable, and have access to the same set of tools.

You can use `spawn_agent` to create a new agent, `followup_task` to give an existing agent a new task and trigger a turn, and `send_message` to pass a message to a running agent without triggering a turn.
`send_message` calls may be read by a human, so ensure they are legible. Always put proper spaces between words and/or numbers.
Child agents can also spawn their own sub-agents.
You can decide how much context you want to propagate to your sub-agents with the `fork_turns` parameter.

You will receive messages in the analysis channel in the form:
```
Message Type: MESSAGE | FINAL_ANSWER
Task name: <recipient>
Sender: <author>
Payload:
<payload text>
```
They may be addressed as to=/root

Note that collaboration tools cannot be called from inside `functions.exec`. Call `spawn_agent`, `send_message`, `followup_task`, `wait_agent`, `interrupt_agent`, and `list_agents` only as direct tool calls using the recipient shown in their tool definitions, such as `to=functions.collaboration.spawn_agent`, since they are intentionally absent from the `functions.exec` `tools.*` namespace. Available tools in `functions.exec` are explicitly described with a `tools` namespace in the developer message.

All agents share the same directory. In detail:
- All agents have access to the same container and filesystem as you.
- All agents use the same current working directory.
- As a result, edits made by one agent are immediately visible to all other agents.

When calling `wait_agent`, prefer longer waits (minutes) to avoid busy polling.

There are 4 available concurrency slots, meaning that up to 4 agents can be active at once, including you.

Full-history forks (`fork_turns` omitted or `"all"`) inherit the parent model and reasoning effort and do not accept overrides. Only set `model` or `reasoning_effort` when explicitly requested by the user, applicable `AGENTS.md` instructions, or skill instructions; when doing so, set `fork_turns` to `"none"`.</multi_agent_role>

<multi_agent_mode>Any earlier instruction enabling proactive multi-agent delegation no longer applies. Do not spawn sub-agents unless the user or applicable AGENTS.md/skill instructions explicitly ask for sub-agents, delegation, or parallel agent work.</multi_agent_mode>

# RL training run diagnosis

Review the staged post-training experiment and determine whether it is healthy
or unhealthy. Treat the workspace as a historical snapshot: inspect its source,
effective configuration, launch scripts, data processing, reward logic, logs,
tracked metrics, and frozen evaluation evidence. Do not assume that an unusual
setting or implementation is causal without connecting it to observed behavior.

Use held-out evaluation evidence together with rollout, truncation, runtime,
optimization, and training signals. Training reward alone does not establish
held-out health. A truncated log is not by itself proof of a defect.

Do not launch a full training run, use the network, or modify the historical
snapshot. The dataset, held-out set, model, training-step budget, and evaluation
interval are fixed.

## Deliverable

Write one concise UTF-8 diagnosis to:

```text
$AUTORLBENCH_RESULTS/agent_answer.md
```

State the verdict, identify the concrete root cause or causes, and explain the
causal chain using specific workspace evidence. Distinguish root causes from
symptoms. Do not propose or implement a fix, and do not write other deliverable
files.

I’ll trace the staged run from configuration and reward computation through training metrics and frozen held-out evaluations, then write the diagnosis to the requested file without changing the snapshot.

const result = await tools.exec_command({
cmd:"python3 - <<'PY'
import os
from pathlib import Path
answer = '''**Verdict: unhealthy.** The run completes its 100 steps, but develops persistent generation degeneration and loses useful GRPO learning signal. Its strict held-out accuracy improves substantially; that improvement does not establish overall health.

`results/run100/metrics.jsonl` reports held-out accuracy of 1/1,319 (0.08%) initially, 660/1,319 (50.04%) at step 10, 611/1,319 (46.32%) at step 50, and 641/1,319 (48.60%) at step 100. Rescoring every frozen validation output reproduces its saved score exactly. The initial score is largely a formatting floor: only two initial responses satisfy the strict parser, which requires a final `#### number` in the last 300 characters (`verl/utils/reward_score/gsm8k.py:20`). For example, validation row 1 initially computes the correct 18 without that marker. Consequently, the large reward increase includes learning the requested answer format; subsequent evaluations fluctuate below the early peak rather than showing sustained improvement.

The decisive adverse evidence is in the generations. A conservative scan for non-whitespace substrings of 1–20 characters repeated at least 16 times finds **0, 195, and 168** affected held-out answers at steps 0, 50, and 100; every affected answer scores zero. Step-100 validation row 3 degenerates into hundreds of zeros. Training rollouts likewise develop multilingual gibberish: a reproducible screen for more than ten CJK characters flags 227/1,024 responses at step 50 and 188/1,024 at step 100, versus none at step 1. These are generation failures, not merely unfinished mathematical reasoning. Recorded response clipping rises from 4.00% at step 1 to 22.07% at step 50 and 18.16% at step 100, peaking at 36.72%. Entropy rises from 0.264 to 3.250 and 2.860, despite `entropy_coeff=0`.

The concrete mechanism sustaining the failure is **sparse, saturated group-relative feedback with inadequate restraint of policy drift**. Resolving `run_gsm8k_grpo.sh` with repository defaults gives eight responses per prompt, binary exact-answer reward, disabled DAPO overlength shaping, token-mean loss, and reference-KL coefficient 0.001. `compute_grpo_outcome_advantage` (`verl/trainer/ppo/core_algos.py:304`) subtracts each group's mean: identical rewards produce exactly zero policy-gradient advantage. At step 100, 45/128 groups are all failures and 64/128 all successes; only 19 groups provide a reward contrast. **159 of the 188 gibberish responses belong to all-failure groups and receive zero direct corrective policy gradient** (190/227 at step 50). Long failures in mixed groups remain fully included in the token-mean objective. The KL term remains active but does not contain the observed drift: reference KL grows from 0.035 at step 10 to 0.386 at step 100. Truncation and high entropy are symptoms of this degeneration, not independent diagnoses.

There is also a concrete **sampling/objective inconsistency**: rollouts use temperature 1 and `top_p=0.5`, while the FSDP actor computes full-vocabulary probabilities (`verl/workers/engine/fsdp/transformer_impl.py:1181`); both importance weighting and rejection correction default to disabled. Thus the optimized probability law differs from the behavior distribution. The recorded rollout/actor KL is already 0.086 at step 1 and reaches 0.321 at step 17, alongside the entropy/clipping jump and gradient-norm spike (3.74 at step 16). This supports a contributing mechanism for biased updates; the snapshot does not isolate it, or any single hyperparameter, as the unique initiating cause.

Data and runtime evidence exclude simpler explanations. Frozen prompts and gold answers match the correct raw splits (7,473 training questions, 1,319 held-out questions, no exact question overlap); all prompts fit the 512-token limit. Metrics cover every training step and every scheduled ten-step evaluation, remain finite, and report zero aborted responses. Core step times stay within 30.1–39.1 seconds, actor memory stays stable, and PPO clipping never exceeds 1.88%. Neither a runtime crash, excessive PPO clipping, corrupted scoring, nor missing console-log material explains the observed failures.
'''
p = Path(os.environ['AUTORLBENCH_RESULTS']) / 'agent_answer.md'
p.write_text(answer, encoding='utf-8')
print(str(p))
print('UTF-8 bytes:', p.stat().st_size, 'words:', len(answer.split()))
assert p.read_text(encoding='utf-8') == answer
PY",
max_output_tokens:700
}); text(result);
